Juvenile Collared large-eye bream (Gymnocranius audleyi) recruit to nearshore seagrass beds at a surprisingly diminutive size, with newly settled individuals weighing just 0.0003 grams [Wwb = 0.0003 grams]. This minimal wet weight at birth, characteristic of many iteroparous lethrinids, reflects the production of numerous small pelagic eggs from which yolk-sac larvae emerge and subsequently undergo a period of rapid, high-mortality growth before settlement. The immediate post-settlement phase is a critical bottleneck, as the tiny recruits must transition to feeding on small benthic invertebrates to fuel their development toward the juvenile stage. Field surveys indicate that this species attains puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, at a total length of 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters]. This length at puberty is relatively modest for a member of the Lethrinidae, suggesting a life-history strategy that favours an early onset of reproductive capability, potentially as a bet-hedging response to variable recruitment success in the dynamic reef environments it inhabits. The timing of this developmental milestone is crucial for understanding population dynamics, as it determines the minimum size at which individuals contribute to the next generation.

The ultimate total length achieved by Gymnocranius audleyi has been recorded at 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], establishing it as a medium-sized species within its genus. This asymptotic size, derived from length-frequency analyses of adult fish from the Great Barrier Reef, provides a key benchmark for parameterizing growth models. The corresponding ultimate female wet weight, based on a length-weight relationship derived from conspecifics and similar-bodied lethrinids, is estimated to be 1225 grams [Wwi = 1225 grams]. This substantial adult body mass is consistent with a dietary shift from small crustaceans to larger, harder-shelled prey such as gastropods and hermit crabs. The allometric exponent used in this estimation (approximately 2.97) indicates that body mass increases in near-cubic proportion to length, a pattern typical of fishes with a robust, deep-bodied morphology that remains consistent throughout the post-settlement phase. Reaching this maximum size appears to require several years of sustained growth in productive habitats.

Reproductive output in Collared large-eye bream has been extrapolated from fecundity data available for the closely related species Lethrinus lentjan. Under stable thermal conditions typical of tropical reef waters, measured at 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], mature females produce approximately 77,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 77,000 eggs per year]. This annual egg production rate represents a composite of batch spawning events over an extended breeding season, a common strategy among tropical spariform fishes that spreads reproductive risk across time. The estimate assumes that a sexually mature female engages in repeated spawning bouts throughout the year when water temperatures remain elevated. The reliance on a congeneric model for this parameter introduces some uncertainty, but the value is considered representative given the phylogenetic and ecological similarity between the two species. Such a sustained, high rate of annual gamete release necessitates substantial energetic investment, which is supported by the abundant prey resources found in the species' preferred coral rubble and sandy flat habitats.

The maximum lifespan documented for Gymnocranius audleyi in wild populations is 4745 days [am = 4745 days], a value recorded under the same ambient temperature regime of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C] at which its reproductive parameters were assessed. This longevity, equivalent to approximately thirteen years, positions the species as a moderately long-lived member of the Lethrinidae. Such a lifespan is consistent with a slow-to-moderate pace of life, wherein the energetic costs of attaining a large adult body size are amortized over many years of reproductive activity. The oldest individuals in a population are typically those that have evaded predation and fishing pressure, accumulating growth increments that push them toward the observed asymptotic length of 40 centimeters. The ecosystem role of these senescent adults, which can exert a disproportionate influence on prey communities due to their size and experience, is an understudied aspect of the species' ecology.

Comparative demographic analyses reveal that the size at first reproduction in Collared large-eye bream, occurring at 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters] in total length, represents a significant ontogenetic gate. At this threshold, individuals shift from a purely somatic growth phase to one that balances energy allocation between further increases in length and the production of gametes. The estimated approximately 77,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 77,000 eggs per year] produced by a prime-aged adult, set within the context of a thirteen-year lifespan, implies a lifetime fecundity that can exceed several hundred thousand eggs. This prodigious output is typical of marine teleosts that broadcast spawn and experience extremely high mortality during the pelagic larval phase. Management strategies for this species must therefore consider the protection of spawning aggregations and the maintenance of sufficient adult biomass to ensure that the total reproductive output of the population remains resilient to environmental stochasticity and fishing pressure.
